title: Why COP31 Ended Without a Climate Deal
seoTitle: Why COP31 Collapsed: Climate Deal Fails Explained
excerpt: COP31 ended without a climate pact on 22 November 2026. Here is why the talks failed, what was in the draft, and what happens next.
content:
What Happened at COP31?

COP31 ended on 22 November 2026 in Antalya, Türkiye, without a climate pact. Negotiators from nearly 200 countries failed to agree on a final text after two weeks of talks and two days of overtime, when the European Union, Pacific island nations and others rejected a draft they said was too weak on fossil fuels. UN Secretary-General António Guterres called the outcome deeply disappointing. The summit ran 44 hours past its scheduled close, the longest UN climate conference on record. The last time a COP's main political agreement collapsed in this way was in Copenhagen in 2009.

Why Did COP31 Fail to Reach a Deal?

The central obstacle was language on fossil fuels. The final draft, called the Antalya Pact, reaffirmed the 1.5 degrees Celsius goal and called for deep, rapid emissions cuts, but it did not explicitly mention moving away from coal, oil and gas. Several countries objected, saying the text weakened earlier commitments and ignored the pace of warming. Differences over climate finance for poorer countries deepened the divide, and co-presidents Türkiye and Australia circulated multiple compromise drafts without winning consensus.

Who Led the COP31 Negotiations?

COP31 was co-hosted by Türkiye and Australia, an unusual arrangement agreed after both countries withdrew rival bids to host. Murat Kurum, Türkiye's environment minister, served as COP president and chair of the negotiations, while Chris Bowen, Australia's climate change minister, acted as president of negotiations. At the closing plenary, Kurum said there was no agreement on the text, so the decisions were not adopted. Bowen pointed to unbridgeable red lines and what he called the most complicated geopolitical environment in living memory.

What Did the Antalya Pact Contain?

The draft cover decision kept the 1.5 degrees Celsius temperature goal and set a target of raising electricity's share of global final energy consumption to 35 percent by 2035. It also proposed scaling up carbon capture, utilisation and storage to gigatonne levels, and acknowledged that temperatures are expected to exceed 1.5 degrees in the coming years. It warned that the remaining carbon budget is shrinking fast and recognised growing loss and damage. What it did not do is set out a clear pathway for phasing down fossil fuels, the main cause of warming.

What Did Guterres Say After the Collapse?

Guterres used his final COP before stepping down to criticise what he called powerful fossil fuel interests taking a page from Big Tobacco's playbook, distorting science and delaying policy. He stressed that the failure changed nothing about the physical reality of climate change. There may be no consensus in the negotiating room, he said, but there is no ambiguity in the science. He pointed to record temperatures, intensifying impacts and emissions that remain far too high, and noted the world is now on course to exceed the 1.5 degrees limit.

What Was Agreed Despite the Collapse?

The failure applied to the overarching political text, not to every negotiating track. A separate decision on the Just Transition Work Programme was adopted, though civil society groups said it fell short of a fully developed mechanism with dedicated resources and worker participation. Several individual climate commitments and side agreements also moved forward. Delegates from countries such as India signalled they would keep working through multilateral talks while insisting that implementation reflect equity and the obligations of developed nations.

How Does COP31 Compare to Past Summits?

COP31 was the first annual UN conference to formally discuss how a key Paris Agreement target would be missed. The UN now estimates current government policies point to roughly 2.8 degrees Celsius of warming by 2100, far above the 1.5 degrees countries set in 2015. While the 2015 Paris deal drove near-universal climate action, the gap between pledges and delivery has widened. Previous COPs have produced landmark deals such as Paris, and others have limped along; COP31 sits at the disappointing end of that spectrum.

What Happens to Climate Action After COP31?

A failed summit does not pause national policy. Countries still submit Nationally Determined Contributions under the Paris Agreement, and those plans are reviewed every five years through the Global Stocktake. The UNFCCC secretariat continues technical work on measuring, reporting and verifying emissions. Bilateral and regional initiatives carry on. What the collapse removes is the signal of a united global political direction, which can slow coordination and weaken the pressure on laggards.

Can a Failed COP Be Reversed?

History suggests a collapse is rarely final. The 2009 Copenhagen summit was widely judged a failure, yet its elements fed into later agreements and eventually the Paris deal. Drafts rejected in one session are often revisited in subsequent meetings, and the co-presidents can carry text forward informally. What matters is whether governments return with the political will to bridge the fossil fuel and finance divides that proved unbridgeable in Antalya.

In India

India arrived at COP31 pushing for predictable climate finance, a just transition and voluntary adaptation metrics, while resisting new top-down mitigation targets. In its official statement, New Delhi cited the duty of developed countries under Article 9.1 of the Paris Agreement to help finance both emissions cuts and adaptation, and asked for grants and cheaper loans rather than market-rate lending. Analysts at the Centre for Policy Research said domestic public finance still supplies about 94.5 percent of tracked adaptation flows in India, underlining how little external money reaches projects on the ground. The Reserve Bank of India has estimated the cumulative cost of adapting to climate change in India at ₹85.6 lakh crore at 2011-12 prices by 2030, a figure reported by The Hindu in May 2023. For Indian readers, the practical takeaway is that national schemes, not the UN text, will drive most near-term action. India's renewable build-out and city heat plans continue regardless of the Antalya outcome.

In Other Countries

In the United States, the federal position on climate has shifted with each administration, so states such as California and New York have carried much of the policy load. The United Kingdom has baked a legally binding target into law and continues to expand offshore wind, giving it a domestic framework that does not depend on COP outcomes. Pacific island nations, though small, wielded outsized influence at COP31 by arguing that a 1.5 degrees world is existential for them, and their objection helped sink the draft. For fossil-fuel-exporting economies, the absence of explicit phase-down language was a relief; for climate-vulnerable states, it was a betrayal.

What the Deal Fight Looked Like

The table below summarises the main points of contention at COP31 and where the draft landed on each. It reflects the state of the text as reported by UN News and Reuters on 22 November 2026.

Frequently Asked Questions

When did COP31 end?

COP31 closed on 22 November 2026 after running 44 hours beyond its scheduled finish, making it the longest UN climate summit on record.

Where was COP31 held?

The talks took place in Antalya, Türkiye, with Australia co-hosting and leading the formal negotiations through climate minister Chris Bowen.

What is the Antalya Pact?

It was the draft cover decision at COP31. It kept the 1.5 degrees goal and set a 35 percent electricity target for 2035, but omitted direct language on moving away from fossil fuels.

Why did the EU reject the COP31 deal?

The European Union and Pacific island nations said the final draft was too weak, pointing to the absence of any reference to fossil fuels and the lack of firm finance commitments from wealthy countries.

Does a failed COP stop climate action?

No. Countries continue with their national climate plans under the Paris Agreement, and domestic policies such as renewable energy targets keep moving. What is lost is coordinated global direction.
